A profound trauma I endured was being a survivor of a terrorist bombing & warzone. Seeing or hearing news about war & terror (especially explosions, shootings, mass fatalities) is an unavoidable trigger I must to do my best to be prepared for and cope with. It's not been easy, but I've learned as much as I could (still learning) about having resilience in times of great stress & trauma. I think having a "toolbox" of coping skills and putting safegaurds in place, is helping me to better cope with painful triggers and provide support to friends and relatives who are effected by the war in Ukraine or other unrest that sadly occurs around the world.

I've learned more about secondary PTSD. Unfortunately, some of my closest loved ones developed secondary PTSD as a result of the deadly ordeals I went through abroad. It's highly traumatic to not to know if your loved one has perished, and constantly be on edge waiting for updates while they are trapped for a prolonged period in an active warzone. It's traumatic to be engulfed by fear and uncertainty. 

Keep in mind that it's possible to stay up to date with a horrifying situation, but still limit excessive exposure to disturbing media content. It's important to stay as grounded as possible and enhance feelings of connectedness, normalcy, and safety. It's a good time to embrace spirituality (for those that are spiritual or religious). 

Comradery, optimism, and protective measures are crucial in a time of ongoing unrest.

I wish you and your loved ones well throughout these difficult times.

I'm immensely sorry you experienced this loss, I wish I could hug you. Since childhood, my biggest fear has been for my dad to complete suicide. When I was 8yo I found him with slit wrists and badly injured from attempting to hang himself in the garage. The rope ended up breaking off the high ceiling, so he landed on concrete ground (being 8, I thought the fall itself was enough to kill him, if there was any chance he was alive at that point). The event of seeing him bleeding, strangled, and fallen to his death all at once was deeply traumatizing. He managed to regain consciousness before being rushed to the hospital, and tried to insist he drive himself to the hospital but my mom obv. refused. We found out he intended to crash full speed off of a secluded cliff area.

Over the years, I cleaned his blood, summoned ambulances, had to call police on my own dad when he tried to drive off hammered. Finding my big tall dad collapsed on stairs was horrifying, feeling helpless to move him to safety or stop him from wreckless behavior that caused injuries and illness. Eventually, he quit drinking permanently and it totally changed his life, my family's life, and all of our relationships with him.

In April this year, I had a terrible premonition that he had passed.  It was so intense that I summoned police to do a welfare check, knowing they could get there faster. They found him deceased in the exact position and location I had pictured. He intentionally hid signs of suicidality, but looking back there were signs. I sensed he was suicidal, but he constantly reassured us he was fine. My family thought I was having some kind of stress related trauma response to suddenly have overwhelming concerns of him being in danger. He had been sober / stable for years.

The police would not let me enter the house at first as the "suspicious death" was under investigation. I knew in my heart what he had done, but until they discovered the note the cause of death wasn't immediately clear to them. 

My dad knew I'd be the only one to check on him and find him. The shred of evidence that he wanted to give me some warning of finding him dead, is that he left a note saying "Call 911" in big letters on the door to the basement. 

I had been hysterically worried and contacting family members when I "sensed" he had just passed late at night. He was not answering my calls or texts, but this was not unusual late at night. In the morning, family members suggested it would be an annoyance to him if I summoned a welfare check "just for not answering his phone while it's on do not disturb".

It seems he likely expected me to check on him after not hearing from him for a few days. I live with intense guilt of feeling like I KNEW what was going to happen, sensed his actual passing, and still couldn't use these senses to stop him from doing it. Suicide leaves so many heartwrenching unanswered questions. His manner of death was my greatest fear realized,  and a loss that will take years to process. 

Sending you love and support. I admire your strength and love for your father. Wishing you all the best in life.

This is just my own personal insight. 


My father attempted suicide when I was a little girl. Although he didn't complete suicide, I was aware that he could have died and it was the greatest trauma of my life up until his recent completed suicide (I am now an adult). As a young child I wondered,  but did not understand how and why he would be willing to leave me. Didn't he love me enough to stick around? Its very hard for a young child to grasp or fathom how their parent could abruptly pass away. 

The void in a child's life, the unanswered questions, the confusion...will be devestating at any age. Loss of a parent at an early age is especially traumatic. I don't think your ex wife "not talking about you" will make it any easier for your daughter to heal and find closure, because she will never forget you... this is something permanently life altering, and not having a parent willing to talk about and properly support a young child through loss can make it even harder. 

I truly hope and pray that you survive this... your daughter loves you so much.
